acts.genre: Short talk · given from notes, about two minutes
acts.title: How we decide
text: Hello, everyone. My name is Stuart French, and I’m here to talk to you about something we all do about seventy times a day — make a decision.
Obviously some are more straightforward than others. Most people don’t have much trouble deciding what to have for breakfast. Some decisions are trickier.

So, in today’s talk I’m going to look at how understanding the decision-making process can help us decide better. First, I want to tell you about some factors that affect our decision-making. Then I’ll talk about the methods people use. And finally, I’ll give you some tips.

The first thing I’d like to mention is the sheer number of decisions we make. Research suggests that making conscious decisions makes the brain tired. So if you have an important decision to make, it’s best to make it early in the day.
Another major factor is how much information we have. Some information is obviously useful. However, if we have too much of it, we are more likely to choose wrongly.
The third and last factor I want to mention is stress. People deciding under stress think more about the possible positive results and less about the negative ones.

To sum up: fewer decisions, less information than you think you need, and not while you are under pressure. Don’t expect everybody to agree with your decisions. Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?

acts.genre: Register · a talk or an essay
acts.title: Spoken from notes, or written to be read?
text: A talk is heard once. It repeats its structure out loud, uses short sentences and speaks directly to the audience.
An essay is read, and can be re-read. It uses longer sentences, written linkers, and never says “thank you for listening”.

tts: Hello everyone. My name is Stuart French and I’m here to talk to you about something we all have to do about seventy times every day — make a decision.
Obviously some are more straightforward than others. Most people don’t have too much trouble deciding what to have for breakfast, but some decisions can be a lot trickier.
So, in today’s talk I’m going to look at how understanding the decision-making process can help us to make better decisions when we really need to.
First, I want to tell you about some factors that affect our decision-making. Then I’ll talk about methods people use to make decisions. And finally, I’ll give you some tips about decision-making.

items.s: He introduces himself and names the topic.
He says we make about seventy decisions a day.
He says some decisions are much harder than others.
He says the talk will cover the factors first.

tts: So, what factors affect our decision-making? The first thing I’d like to mention is the number of decisions we make. Recent research seems to show that making conscious decisions actually makes the brain feel tired. As we make more and more decisions, we become less effective. So if you have an important decision to make, it’s probably best to do it early in the day.

Another major factor is how much information we have to consider. It is obviously a good idea to have some information. However, studies show that if we have too much information to deal with, we are more likely to make the wrong decision.

The third and last factor I want to mention today is stress. Researchers have found that people making decisions under stress are more likely to think about the possible positive results and less likely to think about the negatives.

write.q: Prepare NOTES for a two-minute talk on something you know well. Write notes only — a topic line, three headings with three or four words under each, and one closing line. Do not write out full sentences: you are going to speak from this.
write.model:
TOPIC: why our response time to enquiries matters

1. WHERE THE TIME GOES
– 4 hrs average · nobody owns the inbox · weekends

2. WHAT IT COSTS
– 1 in 3 never replies again · competitors answer in 20 min

3. WHAT WE CHANGE
– one owner per morning · template library · 30-min target

CLOSE: not a technology problem — a rota problem

speak.q: Now give the talk out loud from your notes — about two minutes. Do not read a script. Open with “I’m here to talk to you about…”, name your three parts, signpost each one, and finish with “To sum up…” and “Are there any questions?”
speak.model: Good morning. I’m here to talk to you about something that costs us more money than anything else on the sales team — how long we take to answer a new enquiry. First of all, I’ll show you where the time actually goes. Then let’s move on to what it costs us. And finally I’ll tell you what I think we should change. So, first: the average is four hours, and the reason is simply that nobody owns the inbox in the morning… To sum up: this is not a technology problem, it is a rota problem. Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?
